newsitem.title: POLAND: Poland drops planned change in motor insurance.
newsitem.headline: Poland drops planned change in motor insurance.

text.p: Poland's finance ministry has abandoned its plans to require insured persons to contribute part of the damages payments in motor accident liability cases, Rzeczpospolita daily reported on Wednesday.

The ministry proposal late last year prompted Poland's two largest insurers, the state-owned Powszechny Zaklad Ubezpieczen SA (PZU) and the listed TUiR Warta to lower earlier-announced increases in obligatory motor liability insurance premiums.
"In the end the earlier proposal of introducing the so-called self-participation was abandoned," Rzeczpospolita quoted Anatol Adamski, the finance ministry's insurance adviser, as saying.
But he said the ministry now proposed, in a newly-drafted regulation, to make people who cause repeated accidents pay three times more than others for insurance.

PZU, which in December announced it would increase its premiums by 43 percent but after the ministry's proposal decided to cut it to 33 percent, said it would calculate after the first quarter whether to increase the premiums again.
"We will see, we have to calculate, if there is any decision it will be after we see the first quarter financial data," PZU spokesman Marek Maszek told Reuters.
Warta's spokesman said the firm's management had not yet taken any decisions in the light of the ministry's change of plan, but they might do so in the next few days.

"The management of Warta could make a decision on a possible change in the motor liability insurance in the next few days...one has to take into account that the government's proposals did not materialise," Warta's Jacek Likowski said.
Warta had increased its motor liability insurance in December by 33 percent, then cut the increase by 5-7 percentage points.

Likowski stressed there was no data available in Poland of drivers who cause more accidents than others which meant that the government's new proposal -- to make such people pay more -- could not be implemented.
